title: Photosynthesis
description: The word equation and requirements of photosynthesis, the uses of the carbohydrates made, the roles of nitrate and magnesium ions, the controlled investigations for light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll, the pondweed and hydrogencarbonate indicator practicals, and dicot leaf structure for IGCSE Biology 0610.

notes.heading: The Word Equation — Learn It Exactly
notes.body:
📌 Definition (syllabus 6.1.1)
**Photosynthesis** is the process by which plants **synthesise carbohydrates from raw materials using energy from light**.

🔑 The word equation (6.1.2)
**carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen**
(in the presence of **light** and **chlorophyll**)
Light and chlorophyll are written ABOVE/BELOW the arrow in the exam — they are the conditions of the reaction, NOT reactants. The raw materials are carbon dioxide and water; the products are glucose and oxygen.

🔑 Chlorophyll and chloroplasts (6.1.3, 6.1.4)
**Chlorophyll** is the **green pigment found in chloroplasts**. Its job is to **transfer light energy into chemical energy** — the chemical energy is stored in the carbohydrate (glucose) that is made. That energy-transfer sentence is the marking point, so learn it word for word.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Putting light or chlorophyll on the left of the equation as if they were raw materials. They are not consumed. (The balanced symbol equation is a Supplement objective — it is covered in the plant physiology topic; Core only requires this word equation.)

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Raw materials: carbon dioxide + water. Products: glucose + oxygen.
• Chlorophyll = green pigment in chloroplasts; it transfers light energy into chemical energy.

notes.heading: What the Plant Does With the Carbohydrate (6.1.5)
notes.body:
The glucose made in photosynthesis has several fates. The 0610 Core list has five, and examiners love a 'state two uses' question:

• **Respiration** — glucose is broken down in respiration to release energy for the plant's cells.
• **Starch** — glucose is converted to **starch, an energy store**. Starch is insoluble, so it can be stored in cells without upsetting their water balance (unlike soluble glucose).
• **Cellulose** — glucose is built into **cellulose for cell walls**, strengthening every plant cell.
• **Sucrose** — glucose is converted to sucrose, the soluble sugar **transported in the phloem** to the rest of the plant.
• **Nectar** — flowers make sugary **nectar to attract insects** for pollination.

🔑 What the examiner wants
Match the carbohydrate to its job: storage = starch; structure = cellulose; transport = sucrose; energy release = glucose in respiration; attracting insects = nectar.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'plants store glucose'. Plants store the INSOLUBLE carbohydrate starch; glucose is soluble and reactive, so it is converted before storage or transport.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Five uses: respiration, starch store, cellulose walls, sucrose transport, nectar.
• Starch is the store because it is insoluble.

notes.heading: Mineral Ions: Nitrate and Magnesium (6.1.6)
notes.body:
Photosynthesis makes carbohydrate — but a healthy plant also needs mineral ions absorbed from the soil by the roots. Two are named on the Core syllabus:

• **Nitrate ions** — needed to make **amino acids**, which are then joined together to make proteins for growth.
• **Magnesium ions** — needed to make **chlorophyll**, the green pigment that captures light energy.

🔑 The deficiency link (how examiners test it)
• A plant short of nitrate cannot make enough amino acids → poor, stunted growth.
• A plant short of magnesium cannot make chlorophyll → the leaves turn **yellow** (they lose their green colour), and with less chlorophyll the rate of photosynthesis falls.

💡 Worked Example
A plant kept in bright light with plenty of carbon dioxide and water still has yellow leaves and is growing slowly. Both nitrate and magnesium deficiency fit the symptoms — but 'yellow leaves' specifically points to MAGNESIUM, because the yellow colour is the visible sign of missing chlorophyll.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying 'minerals give the plant energy'. Mineral ions are raw materials for making molecules (amino acids, chlorophyll) — energy comes from respiration of glucose.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Nitrate → amino acids → proteins (growth).
• Magnesium → chlorophyll; deficiency = yellow leaves.

notes.heading: Testing a Leaf for Starch — and Destarching First
notes.body:
Every investigation of photosynthesis at Core ends the same way: testing a leaf for starch, because starch only appears where photosynthesis has happened.

🔑 The starch test method — learn the steps WITH the reasons
1. **Boil the leaf in water** — kills the cells and breaks down the membranes so iodine can enter.
2. **Boil the leaf in ethanol** (heat the ethanol in a water bath — ethanol is flammable, never use a naked flame) — **removes the chlorophyll**, decolourising the leaf so the iodine colour change can be seen.
3. **Rinse in water** — softens the brittle leaf.
4. **Add iodine solution** — **blue-black = starch present**; the iodine stays yellow-brown = no starch.

🔑 Destarching — the step the whole investigation depends on
Before the experiment, the plant is kept in the dark for 24–48 hours. With no light there is no photosynthesis, and the leaves use up or export their stored starch — the plant is **destarched**. This guarantees that any starch found at the end was made DURING the experiment, so a positive test really is evidence about the variable you changed.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting why ethanol is used: it removes chlorophyll (the green colour), it does not test for starch. And never heat ethanol directly over a Bunsen flame — it catches fire; use a water bath.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Boil in water → boil in ethanol (water bath) → rinse → iodine.
• Blue-black = starch; destarch first so results are valid.

notes.heading: Controlled Investigations: Chlorophyll, Light and Carbon Dioxide (6.1.7)
notes.body:
The three classic Core investigations each test whether ONE requirement is needed — and each needs a **control**: a set-up identical except for the factor being tested.

🔑 Chlorophyll — the variegated leaf
Take a destarched plant with **variegated leaves** (green parts containing chlorophyll, white parts without) and leave it in the light. On testing, only the GREEN areas turn blue-black → **chlorophyll is needed** for photosynthesis. The white areas of the SAME leaf are the built-in control — light, carbon dioxide and water are the same for both areas.

🔑 Light — the foil strip
Cover part of a destarched leaf with aluminium foil, leaving the rest exposed, and keep the plant in the light. Only the UNCOVERED part turns blue-black → **light is needed**. The covered strip of the same leaf is the control.

🔑 Carbon dioxide — the absorber
Enclose a destarched plant (or leaf) with **potassium hydroxide (KOH), which absorbs carbon dioxide** from the air around the leaf; a second plant is set up identically WITHOUT the absorber (the control). After time in the light, the plant without KOH tests positive for starch and the plant with KOH does not → **carbon dioxide is needed**.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Describing the experiment without saying what the control is. 'Compare with a leaf kept in the dark' scores nothing unless you say everything else was kept the same.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• One variable changed, everything else the same = a valid control.
• KOH absorbs CO₂; foil blocks light; white areas of a variegated leaf lack chlorophyll.

notes.heading: Measuring the Rate: Pondweed and the Hydrogencarbonate Indicator (6.1.8–6.1.9)
notes.body:
🔑 The pondweed practical
Photosynthesis releases oxygen, so the rate can be measured in an aquatic plant (pondweed, e.g. Elodea) by **counting the oxygen bubbles released per minute**. Investigate one factor at a time:
• **Light intensity** — move a lamp to different distances.
• **Carbon dioxide concentration** — dissolve different amounts of sodium hydrogencarbonate in the water.
• **Temperature** — stand the apparatus in water baths at different temperatures.
Keep every other variable constant, and let the plant adjust for a few minutes before counting.

🔑 Describing the effects (Core level)
• Increasing light intensity → the rate of photosynthesis increases.
• Increasing carbon dioxide concentration → the rate increases.
• Increasing temperature → the rate increases, up to a point.
(Explaining WHY a factor stops having an effect — limiting factors — is a Supplement objective, covered in the plant physiology topic.)

🔑 The hydrogencarbonate indicator
This indicator tracks the carbon dioxide concentration around an aquatic plant: it is **orange-red in normal air, turns yellow when CO₂ rises, and turns purple when CO₂ falls**. Sealed tubes with a plant and indicator show the gas exchange:
• In the DARK: the plant only respires → CO₂ rises → indicator turns **yellow**.
• In the LIGHT: photosynthesis uses CO₂ faster than respiration releases it → CO₂ falls → indicator turns **purple**.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying plants 'only photosynthesise' in the light. They respire all the time; in bright light photosynthesis is simply faster, so CO₂ falls overall.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Rate = bubbles of oxygen per minute; change one variable at a time.
• Indicator: yellow = more CO₂ (dark), purple = less CO₂ (light).

notes.heading: The Dicot Leaf: Structure and Adaptations (6.2)
notes.body:
📌 The two general adaptations (6.2.1)
Leaves are adapted for photosynthesis by having a **large surface area** — to absorb as much light as possible and exchange gases quickly — and by being **thin**, so the diffusion distance for carbon dioxide to reach the photosynthesising cells is short.

🔑 The structures you must identify (6.2.2)
On a dicotyledonous leaf cross-section, be able to label: **cuticle, upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, air spaces, lower epidermis, guard cells and stomata, vascular bundles (veins), xylem and phloem**, and the **chloroplasts** inside the cells.

🔑 Explaining the adaptations (6.2.3) — how each feature earns its place
• **Cuticle** — a waxy, transparent waterproof layer: reduces water loss while still letting light through.
• **Upper epidermis** — transparent, so light passes through to the mesophyll below.
• **Palisade mesophyll** — column-shaped cells near the top of the leaf, **packed with chloroplasts** to trap the most light; the main site of photosynthesis.
• **Spongy mesophyll + air spaces** — the spaces let carbon dioxide diffuse to every photosynthesising cell (and oxygen away).
• **Stomata and guard cells** — stomata are pores (mostly in the lower epidermis) that let carbon dioxide in; the pair of guard cells around each stoma controls its opening.
• **Vascular bundle** — **xylem** brings water (a raw material) to the leaf; **phloem** carries sucrose away to the rest of the plant.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Mixing up palisade and spongy mesophyll: PALISADE = Packed with chloroplasts, near the top. Spongy = Spaces for gas exchange.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Large + thin leaf; palisade traps light; air spaces + stomata move the gases; xylem in, phloem out.

illustration.alt: Labelled cross-section of a dicotyledonous leaf showing the cuticle, upper and lower epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll with chloroplasts and air spaces, guard cells and a stoma, and a vascular bundle with xylem above phloem.
illustration.caption: Every labelled layer is a marking point: palisade cells packed with chloroplasts trap light, air spaces circulate the gases, and the vein's xylem and phloem supply water and remove sucrose.

flashcards.definition: The process by which plants synthesise carbohydrates from raw materials using energy from light.
flashcards.example: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, in the presence of light and chlorophyll.

flashcards.definition: The green pigment found in chloroplasts; it transfers light energy into chemical energy stored in carbohydrate.
flashcards.example: White areas of a variegated leaf contain no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise.

flashcards.definition: The organelle that contains chlorophyll and is the site of photosynthesis.
flashcards.example: Palisade mesophyll cells contain more chloroplasts than any other leaf cells.

flashcards.definition: After boiling the leaf in water and decolourising it in hot ethanol, iodine turns blue-black where starch is present.
flashcards.example: A destarched leaf left in the light turns blue-black; one kept in the dark stays yellow-brown.

flashcards.definition: Keeping a plant in the dark for 24–48 hours before an investigation so all stored starch is used up or exported.
flashcards.example: It guarantees any starch found at the end was made during the experiment itself.

flashcards.definition: A leaf with green and white areas shows that chlorophyll is needed: after time in the light, only the green areas test positive for starch.
flashcards.example: The white areas act as the control — same leaf, same light, same carbon dioxide.

flashcards.definition: A chemical that absorbs carbon dioxide; used to show that CO₂ is needed for photosynthesis.
flashcards.example: A destarched plant sealed with KOH tests negative for starch, while the control plant tests positive.

flashcards.definition: An indicator of carbon dioxide level: orange-red in air, yellow when CO₂ rises, purple when CO₂ falls.
flashcards.example: An aquatic plant in the light turns the indicator purple; in the dark it turns yellow.

flashcards.definition: Mineral ions absorbed from the soil, needed to make amino acids (and therefore proteins).
flashcards.example: Nitrate deficiency causes poor, stunted growth.

flashcards.definition: Mineral ions absorbed from the soil, needed to make chlorophyll.
flashcards.example: Magnesium deficiency turns leaves yellow because chlorophyll cannot be made.

flashcards.definition: The layer of column-shaped cells near the top of the leaf, packed with chloroplasts — the main site of photosynthesis.
flashcards.example: It sits just under the transparent upper epidermis so it receives the most light.

flashcards.definition: Stomata are pores (mostly in the lower epidermis) that let carbon dioxide diffuse in; each stoma is opened and closed by a pair of guard cells.
flashcards.example: Stomata also let oxygen and water vapour out of the leaf.

questions.stem: What are the raw materials of photosynthesis?
choices: Carbon dioxide and water
Glucose and oxygen
Carbon dioxide and oxygen
Glucose and water
questions.explanation: The word equation is carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (in the presence of light and chlorophyll). Glucose and oxygen are the PRODUCTS, not the raw materials.

questions.stem: What is the role of chlorophyll in photosynthesis?
choices: It absorbs water from the soil
It gives flowers their colour to attract insects
It transfers light energy into chemical energy
It absorbs carbon dioxide from the air
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in chloroplasts that transfers light energy into chemical energy stored in carbohydrate. Roots absorb water, and carbon dioxide diffuses in through stomata — neither is chlorophyll's job.

questions.stem: Which carbohydrate made from the products of photosynthesis is transported around the plant in the phloem?
choices: Starch
Sucrose
Cellulose
Chlorophyll
questions.explanation: Sucrose is the soluble sugar transported in the phloem. Starch is the insoluble store, cellulose builds cell walls, and chlorophyll is a pigment, not a carbohydrate.

questions.stem: A plant has plenty of light, water and carbon dioxide, but its leaves are turning yellow and photosynthesis is slow. Which mineral ion is it most likely to be short of?
choices: Nitrate
Calcium
Potassium
Magnesium
questions.explanation: Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll; without them the leaves lose their green colour and photosynthesis slows. Nitrate deficiency stunts growth but the tell-tale yellowing (missing chlorophyll) points to magnesium.

questions.stem: Before investigating whether light is needed for photosynthesis, a plant is kept in the dark for 24–48 hours. Why?
choices: To kill any microorganisms on the leaves
To destarch the plant, so any starch found later must have been made during the experiment
To remove the chlorophyll from the leaves
To make the stomata open wider
questions.explanation: In the dark there is no photosynthesis, so stored starch is used up or exported — the plant is destarched. This makes the final iodine test valid evidence about the variable being investigated. Ethanol (not darkness) removes chlorophyll.

questions.stem: In the starch test, why is the leaf boiled in ethanol after being boiled in water?
choices: To kill the leaf cells
To soften the leaf
To add iodine to the cells
To remove the chlorophyll so the iodine colour change can be seen clearly
questions.explanation: Hot ethanol extracts the green chlorophyll, leaving a pale leaf on which the blue-black iodine colour is easy to see. Boiling in water is what kills the cells and breaks the membranes — the two steps have different purposes.

questions.stem: A destarched plant with variegated (green and white) leaves is left in bright light, then a leaf is tested for starch. Which areas turn blue-black?
choices: Only the green areas
Only the white areas
The whole leaf
Neither area — the plant was destarched
questions.explanation: Only the green areas contain chlorophyll, so only they can photosynthesise and make starch. The white areas are the control: everything else (light, CO₂, water) was the same, so the comparison shows chlorophyll is needed.

questions.stem: Two destarched plants are left in the light. Plant X is sealed in a bag containing potassium hydroxide (KOH); plant Y is sealed in an identical bag without KOH. What is the result of testing their leaves for starch, and what does it show?
choices: Both test positive — sealing the bag makes no difference
Neither tests positive — sealed plants cannot photosynthesise
Only plant Y tests positive — KOH absorbs carbon dioxide, showing CO₂ is needed
Only plant X tests positive — KOH provides extra carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: KOH absorbs carbon dioxide from the air in the bag, so plant X has no CO₂ and cannot photosynthesise. Plant Y is the control — identical apart from the absorber — so its positive test shows that CO₂ is the factor responsible.

questions.stem: A destarched leaf has a strip of aluminium foil fixed over part of it and the plant is left in the light for a day. Which iodine-test result provides evidence that light is needed for photosynthesis?
choices: The whole leaf turns blue-black
The whole leaf stays yellow-brown
Only the covered part turns blue-black
Only the uncovered part turns blue-black
questions.explanation: The foil blocks light, so the covered strip cannot photosynthesise and stays yellow-brown; the uncovered part makes starch and turns blue-black. Because both parts share the same leaf, the covered strip acts as the control.

questions.stem: In the pondweed experiment, a lamp is moved closer to the plant (everything else kept the same). What happens to the rate of bubbling?
choices: It increases — the light intensity is higher, so the rate of photosynthesis is higher
It decreases — the heat from the lamp stops photosynthesis
It stays exactly the same
Bubbling stops because the plant is disturbed
questions.explanation: Moving the lamp closer raises the light intensity, and increasing light intensity increases the rate of photosynthesis — so more oxygen bubbles are released per minute.

questions.stem: A sealed tube containing hydrogencarbonate indicator (orange-red in air) and an aquatic plant is left in the dark for several hours. What colour does the indicator become, and why?
choices: Purple — the plant absorbs carbon dioxide
It stays orange-red — nothing happens without light
Yellow — in the dark the plant only respires, so carbon dioxide rises
Colourless — the indicator breaks down in the dark
questions.explanation: Without light there is no photosynthesis, but respiration continues, releasing CO₂. Rising CO₂ turns the indicator yellow. In the light the same plant would turn it purple as photosynthesis removes CO₂ faster than respiration adds it.

questions.stem: How are palisade mesophyll cells adapted for their role?
choices: They are loosely arranged with large air spaces between them
They sit near the top of the leaf and are packed with chloroplasts to trap light
They form a waterproof layer on the leaf surface
They carry water from the roots to the leaf
questions.explanation: Palisade cells are column-shaped, positioned just under the transparent upper epidermis, and contain more chloroplasts than any other cells — making the palisade layer the main site of photosynthesis. Air spaces belong to the spongy mesophyll; the waterproof layer is the cuticle.

questions.stem: What is the function of the stomata and guard cells in a leaf?
choices: They transport sucrose away from the leaf
They absorb light energy for the mesophyll
The stomata let carbon dioxide diffuse into the leaf, and the guard cells control the opening of each pore
They store starch for the plant
questions.explanation: Stomata are pores (mainly in the lower epidermis) through which CO₂ enters and oxygen and water vapour leave; the pair of guard cells around each stoma controls how open it is. Transport of sucrose is the phloem's job.

questions.stem: Being thin is one of a leaf's two general adaptations for photosynthesis. Why does thinness help?
choices: It makes the leaf lighter so the branch does not break
It gives carbon dioxide a short diffusion distance to reach the photosynthesising cells
It lets water evaporate from the leaf more quickly
It allows more leaves to fit on the plant
questions.explanation: The two general adaptations are a large surface area (to absorb light and exchange gases) and being thin, so the diffusion distance for CO₂ (and O₂) between the air and the mesophyll cells is short and exchange is fast.

questions.stem: Which row correctly matches a leaf structure to its adaptation for photosynthesis?
choices: Cuticle — transparent, so light passes through to the mesophyll while water loss is reduced
Spongy mesophyll — tightly packed cells that trap the most light
Xylem — carries sucrose away from the leaf to the rest of the plant
Stomata — found mainly on the upper surface to absorb more light
questions.explanation: The waxy cuticle is waterproof yet transparent, so light reaches the mesophyll. Tightly packed light-trapping cells are the PALISADE layer (spongy mesophyll has air spaces); sucrose leaves in the PHLOEM (xylem brings water in); and stomata are mainly on the lower epidermis.
